Neonatal gharials emerge from eggs measuring approximately 37 cm [Lb = approximately 37 cm] in total length at birth, a size that reflects the considerable yolk reserves required to support development within the leathery-shelled egg. Field studies indicate that eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] complete development and hatch after an average period of 82 days [ab = 82 days], though reported values range between 71 and 93 days depending on microclimate variation within the nest mound. This incubation duration is typical for large-bodied crocodylians. The egg wet weight itself averages 160 g [Ww0 = averages 160 g], a substantial investment by the gravid female reptile that underscores the species' life-history strategy of producing relatively large offspring. Hatchlings then emerge weighing approximately 130 g [Wwb = approximately 130 g], and their initial size enables them to begin capturing small fish and invertebrates shortly after emergence from the nest.

By eighteen months of age, juveniles in captive rearing programs maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] have attained a total body length of 100 cm , reflecting a period of rapid somatic expansion driven by high food intake rates. This early growth phase is critical for survival, as larger size confers a competitive advantage in basking sites and reduces predation risk from raptors and larger carnivores. The species exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism in adulthood, a pattern common among crocodylians where males attain substantially larger ultimate dimensions. Females reach a maximum recorded total length of 375 cm [Li = 375 cm], whereas males can achieve an ultimate total length of 625 cm [Li = 625 cm]. This divergence in adult body size influences not only foraging ecology—larger males are able to take larger prey items such as riverine mammals—but also social dominance hierarchies along the riverbanks of northern India and Nepal.

Puberty in gharials is marked by the development of the characteristic ghara, or nasal protuberance, in males, which serves both as a vocal resonator and a visual signal of reproductive readiness. Females attain sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 300 cm [Lp = approximately 300 cm], while males typically reach puberty when they have grown to about 350 cm [Lp = about 350 cm] in total length. The age at which females achieve this milestone under natural thermal conditions approximating 23 °C [T = 23 °C] is estimated at roughly 5840 days [tR = roughly 5840 days], based on long-term mark-recapture studies along the Chambal River. This delayed reproductive maturity is consistent with the species' k-selected life-history strategy, which prioritizes adult survival over early reproduction. At this size, females also begin to develop the nesting behavior characteristic of reproductively active adults, selecting sandbanks with specific thermal properties for egg deposition.

Reproductive output in female gharials is size-dependent, with larger individuals producing larger clutches. At a body length of 364 cm, an approximate age of first reproduction for many females, females lay between 20 and 95 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 20 and 95 eggs per clutch], and typically nest every two to three years, yielding an average frequency of approximately 0.37 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.37 clutches per year] under the thermal regime typical of active foraging at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Clutch size varies with maternal body condition and local prey abundance. The nests are excavated in sandy substrates, and the female guards the site throughout the incubation period, which lasts for the previously noted duration.

The maximum lifespan recorded for wild gharials under the prevailing thermal conditions of their riverine habitat, averaging 23 °C [T = 23 °C], is approximately 36,500 days [am = approximately 36,500 days], a longevity that rivals that of larger crocodylids. Such extended lifespans allow for multiple reproductive events across a female's lifetime, offsetting the delayed onset of reproduction. The species' ultimate wet weight for males reaches 977,000 g [Wwi = 977,000 g], a massive body size that requires decades of continuous growth to achieve. This prolonged growth trajectory is supported by the gharial's specialized piscivorous diet and efficient metabolic physiology. Conservation efforts are challenged by the species' low reproductive rate and late maturity, as populations impacted by habitat fragmentation and incidental mortality in fishing nets recover only very slowly. Ongoing captive breeding programs aim to supplement wild populations by releasing head-started juveniles at sizes that improve post-release survival.
